rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast scouting gradient to locate all 10 compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing truncation risk. The midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient unchanged and raise temperature to test selectivity in the crowded middle cluster. All compounds currently elute well within 10 minutes, so improving the critical pairs is the priority.

Use a shallower gradient at the best temperature so far to improve the remaining critical pair and test gradient-dependent selectivity. The current 6.58-minute last peak leaves room to lengthen the gradient while aiming to keep all peaks within 10 minutes.

An intermediate gradient should improve the pair that was under-resolved at 10 minutes while preserving more separation in the pair that worsened at 16 minutes. This targets full resolution with the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.
Injection 4 reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise temperature one grid step to test whether all compounds can elute faster while retaining full resolution.

Return to the successful temperature and raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention. This tests whether the altered gradient window preserves both critical separations while improving on injection 4's elution time.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to recover the critical separation lost when the starting organic fraction increased. This may retain full resolution with a last-peak time close to, or slightly shorter than, injection 4.

Test the low-temperature selectivity regime for a potentially faster fully resolved method, keeping injection 4 as the maximum-score benchmark. The large temperature change may separate the central cluster in a different elution order, while the broad gradient limits excessive retention.

Test a steep gradient at 60 C to see whether the near-coeluting pair crosses elution order and separates again. This explores a substantially faster regime while retaining injection 4 as the fully resolved benchmark.

Explore the fast, high-temperature regime with a higher starting organic fraction to shift selectivity and a longer gradient to ease peak crowding. Injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback while this tests for a shorter fully resolved separation.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the remaining critical pair separates further in this fast regime. Monitor the first pair closely, since increasing starting strength also compresses the early peaks.

Test an intermediate temperature with a shorter gradient to seek a faster fully resolved selectivity window. Restore the low starting organic fraction to avoid the early-peak compression seen in injection 11.

Refine around the maximum-score method with a slightly shallower gradient, aiming to increase the marginal separation of the earlier critical pair. This tests the full-resolution boundary while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test whether a steeper gradient separates the central cluster in the lower-temperature elution-order regime. This explores a substantially faster alternative while retaining injection 4 as the shortest fully resolved method found so far.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction at 50 C improves central-cluster selectivity while shortening retention relative to injection 4. The lower temperature may also preserve early-pair retention better than the 60 C high-starting-strength trial.

Refine the near-perfect injection 7 by reducing the endpoint one grid step, targeting R above 1.5 for its remaining critical pair. This should keep the last peak below 10 minutes and may provide a fully resolved alternative with better minimum-resolution margin.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to recover critical-pair resolution while reducing initial retention. This tests for a fully resolved alternative near the best method’s elution time, with potentially greater separation margin.

Shorten injection 16’s gradient by two minutes while adjusting the endpoint to moderate the slope increase. This targets a faster fully resolved method and tests how much of its critical-pair margin can be traded for time.

Reduce injection 18’s endpoint one step to restore the remaining critical separation. The resulting slope lies between injections 7 and 16, targeting full resolution with a shorter elution time than injection 16.

Test a gradient slope just steeper than injection 4, using the low starting organic fraction that gave the shortest fully resolved separation. This probes whether retention can be shortened while keeping both critical pairs at R ≥ 1.5.

Back off injection 20’s endpoint one step, restoring the successful slope of injection 4 with a shorter programmed gradient. Because all peaks should elute before the gradient ends, this should preserve full resolution and the maximum CRF.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 16 to improve its earlier critical pair while checking that the later pair remains fully resolved. With the maximum CRF already secured, this seeks additional resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 4’s successful slope through the expected last peak at 7.60 minutes. This should retain the maximum CRF with a lower endpoint and shorter gradient, though it is not expected to shorten the elution window.

Shorten the gradient another step while preserving the successful slope through the critical cluster, then hold at 0.50 organic. This tests whether a shorter programmed gradient still achieves maximum CRF; the last peak may elute later during the hold.

Refine injection 17 with a shallower gradient to bring its remaining critical pair above R = 1.5, targeting another maximum-score method with improved resolution margin. Injection 4 remains the shortest fully resolved benchmark; this final trial is expected to keep the last peak below 10 minutes.
